newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION - SUMMARY OF RATIONALE/MAIN ISSUES.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION - SUMMARY OF RATIONALE/MAIN ISSUES.

text.p: Following is summary of main issues ahead of the decisive French second-round parliamentary election vote on June 1 and explanations for having an early election:
EARLY ELECTIONS

- President Jacques Chirac said he called election nearly a year ahead of schedule to give French people a say on the speed and scale of economic reform and put France in a strong position in talks on Europe ahead on the launch of a single currency
- Centre-right win would give Chirac a "friendly" parliament to presidential term end in 2002; left win means "cohabitation", power-sharing with government from different party.
- Under constitution, president cannot dissolve parliament for another year. Normal lifetime of parliament is five years.
VOTING
- Combined left -- Socialist Party and allies plus Communist Party -- led centre-right RPR/UDF ruling coalition in first round on May 25.

- Opinion poll publication banned from week before the first round. Last published polls before round one had consistently shown the RPR/UDF winning a majority of seats in the 577-seat National Assembly but with majority cut.
- 289-seat total required for absolute majority. Socialist party could also run government with Communists/ecologists.
-French TV due to broadcast first projections at 1800 GMT.
LEADERSHIP
- Prime Minister Alain Juppe said after round one defeat he would step down whoever won runoff second round.
- No sucessor named, but National Assembly president Philippe Seguin emerged as a would-be successor between rounds.
- Centre-right round one defeat seen as rejection of Juppe's austerity drive. No new campaign platform proposed to replace one drawn up under Juppe campaign leadership.
- Socialist leader Lionel Jospin widely expected to become prime minister if left wins.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION?
- Socialist party backs EMU but has laid out four conditions which Jospin says are basis of discussion rather than "take it or leave it" conditions.

- Conditions, in manifesto, call for European economic government, flexible interpretation of Maastricht treaty and early Italy/Spain entry, euro which is not overvalued and a new solidarity and growth pact. Jospin says does not feel bound by "stability pact" meant to limit budget deficits under EMU.
- Socialist party says its line will be the line of any left wing government even if it shares power with Communist party, which wants new referendum on EMU.
- centre-right had worked towards a strict interpretation of Maastricht treaty but Juppe said during campaign it too believed in "political" reading of Maastricht and an economic government.
- Seguin, who campaigned against Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum, has softended tone, says France's signature must be honoured, but he wants a softer approach to EMU.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR FRENCH ECONOMIC POLICIES?
- Centre-right policies have become unclear since Juppe announced he would step down. No new platform presented to replace that proposed under Juppe.

- Since the first round, Chirac however has said he wants policies coupling economic liberalism and social protection. These ideas have been embodied by the socially minded Seguin, and Alain Madelin, a economic liberal who been tipped as a possible centre-right finance minister.

- Outgoing Juppe government was committed to curbing state spending to keep rises below inflation, continuing programme of income tax cuts. It had been expected to introduce further austerity expected in 1998 budget and was aiming to fulfil a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.
- Socialist party has said will not impose new austerity just to fulfil a strict reading of Maastricht, but Jospin says it will not raise spending or taxes.
- If it gains power it wants an audit of public finances to establish how much room it has to implement reforms meant to reduce unemployment running at a record 12.8 percent.
- Its manifesto promises goal of creating 700,000 jobs with state support and reducing work week to 35 from 39 hours without cutting pay to increase purchasing power
- room for manoeuvre for any government limited: both sides show general acceptance of need to prevent further rise in state deficit to head of risk of big debt repayments in future.
- the outgoing government delayed partial privatisation of France Telecom, due in May, to June. Position of any new centre-right government on state sales unclear.

- Socialist and Communist parties wary of "privatisation", notably France Telecom, defence group Thomson-CSF and Air France but Socialists may be open to sales of minority stakes. Say will "consult" staff on France Telecom partial sale
